{{Short description|Problem of counting solutions to logic formulas}}
{{Correct title|title=#SAT|reason=hash}}
{{more citations needed|date=June 2019}}
In [[computer science]], the '''Sharp Satisfiability Problem''' (sometimes called '''Sharp-SAT''', '''#SAT''' or '''model counting''') is the problem of counting the number of [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretations]] that [[Satisfiability|satisfy]] a given [[Boolean logic|Boolean]] [[Formula (mathematical logic)|formula]], introduced by Valiant in 1979.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1016/0304-3975(79)90044-6|title=The complexity of computing the permanent|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=8|issue=2|pages=189–201|year=1979|last1=Valiant|first1=L.G.|doi-access=free}}</ref> In other words, it asks in how many ways the variables of a given Boolean formula can be consistently replaced by the values TRUE or FALSE in such a way that the formula [[Validity (logic)|evaluates to TRUE]]. For example, the formula <math>a\lor \neg b</math> is satisfiable by three distinct Boolean value assignments of the variables, namely, for any of the assignments (<math>a</math> = TRUE,  <math>b</math> = FALSE), (<math>a</math> = FALSE, <math>b</math> = FALSE), and (<math>a</math> = TRUE, <math>b</math> = TRUE), we have <math>a\lor \neg b = \textsf{TRUE}.</math>

<nowiki>#</nowiki>SAT is different from [[Boolean satisfiability problem]] (SAT), which asks if there exists ''a solution'' to a Boolean formula. Instead, #SAT asks to enumerate ''all'' ''the solutions'' to a Boolean formula. #SAT is harder than SAT in the sense that, once the total number of solutions to a Boolean formula is known, SAT can be decided in constant time. However, the converse is not true, because knowing a Boolean formula has ''a solution'' does not help us to count ''all the solutions'', as there are an exponential number of possibilities.

<nowiki>#</nowiki>SAT is a well-known example of the class of [[Counting problem (complexity)|counting problems]], known as [[Sharp-P-complete|#P-complete]] (read as sharp P complete). In other words, every instance of a problem in the complexity class [[♯P|#P]] can be reduced to an instance of the #SAT problem. This is an important result because many difficult counting problems arise in [[Enumerative combinatorics|Enumerative Combinatorics]], [[Statistical physics]], Network Reliability, and [[Artificial intelligence]] without any known formula. If a problem is shown to be hard, then it provides a [[Computational complexity theory|complexity theoretic]] explanation for the lack of nice looking formulas.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~salil/cs221/fall02/scribenotes/nov20.pdf|title=Lecture 24: Counting Problems|last=Vadhan|first=Salil Vadhan|date=20 November 2018}}</ref>

== #P-Completeness ==
<nowiki>#</nowiki>SAT is [[♯P-complete|#P-complete]]. To prove this, first note that #SAT is obviously in #P.

Next, we prove that #SAT is #P-hard. Take any problem #A in #P. We know that A can be solved using a [[Non-deterministic Turing machine|Non-deterministic Turing Machine]] M. On the other hand, from the proof for [[Cook-Levin theorem|Cook-Levin Theorem]], we know that we can reduce M to a boolean formula F. Now, each valid assignment of F corresponds to a unique acceptable path in M, and vice versa. However, each acceptable path taken by M represents a solution to A. In other words, there is a bijection between the valid assignments of F and the solutions to A. So, the reduction used in the proof for Cook-Levin Theorem is parsimonious. This implies that #SAT is #P-hard.

==Intractable special cases==

Counting solutions is intractable (#P-complete) in many special cases for which satisfiability is tractable (in P), as well as when satisfiability is intractable (NP-complete). This includes the following.

=== #3SAT ===
This is the counting version of [[3SAT]]. One can show that any formula in SAT [[3SAT|can be rewritten]] as a formula in 3-[[conjunctive normal form|CNF]] form preserving the number of satisfying assignments. Hence, #SAT and #3SAT are counting equivalent and #3SAT is #P-complete as well.

=== #2SAT ===
Even though [[2SAT]] (deciding whether a 2CNF formula has a solution) is polynomial, counting the number of solutions is [[♯P|#P]]-complete.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Valiant | first1 = Leslie G. | author-link = Leslie Valiant
 | year = 1979
 | title = The complexity of enumeration and reliability problems
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Computing]]
 | volume=8
 | pages= 410–421
 | doi = 10.1137/0208032
 | issue = 3}}</ref>
The #P-completeness already in the monotone case, i.e., when there are no [[negation]]s (#MONOTONE-2-CNF).

It is known that, assuming that [[NP (class)|NP]] is different from [[RP (class)|RP]], #MONOTONE-2-CNF also cannot be [[approximation algorithm|approximated]] by a fully [[polynomial-time approximation scheme]] (FPRAS), even assuming that each variable occurs in at most 6 clauses, but that a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) exists when each variable occurs in at most 5 clauses:<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Liu |first1=Jingcheng |last2=Lu |first2=Pinyan |date=2015 |title=FPTAS for Counting Monotone CNF |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611973730.101 |language=en |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |pages=1531–1548 |doi=10.1137/1.9781611973730.101 |isbn=978-1-61197-374-7|arxiv=1311.3728 }}</ref> this follows from analogous results on the problem [[♯IS]] of counting the number of [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]]s in [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]s.

=== #Horn-SAT ===
Similarly, even though [[Horn-satisfiability]] is polynomial, counting the number of solutions is #P-complete. This result follows from a general dichotomy characterizing which SAT-like problems are #P-complete.<ref name="dichotomy">{{Cite journal | title=Complexity of Generalized Satisfiability Counting Problems | year=1996 | last1=Creignou | first1=Nadia | last2=Hermann | first2=Miki | journal=Information and Computation | volume=125 | pages=1–12 | doi=10.1006/inco.1996.0016| hdl=10068/41883 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Planar #3SAT ===
This is the counting version of [[Planar 3SAT]]. The hardness reduction from 3SAT to Planar 3SAT given by Lichtenstein<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lichtenstein|first=David|date=1982|title=Planar Formulae and Their Uses|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing|volume=11|issue=2 |pages=329–343|doi=10.1137/0211025 }}</ref> is parsimonious.  This implies that Planar #3SAT is #P-complete.

=== Planar Monotone Rectilinear #3SAT ===
This is the counting version of Planar Monotone Rectilinear 3SAT.<ref name=":0">{{cite conference
 | last1 = de Berg | first1 = Mark | author1-link = Mark de Berg
 | last2 = Khosravi | first2 = Amirali
 | editor1-last = Thai | editor1-first = My T.
 | editor2-last = Sahni | editor2-first = Sartaj
 | contribution = Optimal binary space partitions in the plane
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-14031-0_25
 | location = Berlin
 | mr = 2720098
 | pages = 216–225
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Computing and Combinatorics: 16th Annual International Conference, COCOON 2010, Nha Trang, Vietnam, July 19-21, 2010, Proceedings
 | volume = 6196
 | year = 2010| isbn = 978-3-642-14030-3 }}</ref> The NP-hardness reduction given by de Berg & Khosravi<ref name=":0" /> is parsimonious. Therefore, this problem is #P-complete as well.

=== #DNF ===

For [[disjunctive normal form]] (DNF) formulas, counting the solutions is also [[#P]]-complete, even when all clauses have size 2 and there are no [[negation]]s: this is because, by [[De Morgan's laws]], counting the number of solutions of a DNF amounts to counting the number of solutions of the negation of a [[conjunctive normal form]] (CNF) formula. Intractability even holds in the case known as #PP2DNF, where the variables are partitioned into two sets, with each clause containing one variable from each set.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Suciu |first1=Dan |chapter=The Query Evaluation Problem |date=2011 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-01879-4_3 |title=Probabilistic Databases |pages=45–52 |editor-last=Suciu |editor-first=Dan |access-date=2023-09-16 |series=Synthesis Lectures on Data Management |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-01879-4_3 |isbn=978-3-031-01879-4 |last2=Olteanu |first2=Dan |last3=Ré |first3=Christopher |last4=Koch |first4=Christoph |editor2-last=Olteanu |editor2-first=Dan |editor3-last=Ré |editor3-first=Christopher |editor4-last=Koch |editor4-first=Christoph|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

By contrast, it is possible to tractably approximate the number of solutions of a disjunctive normal form formula using the [[Karp-Luby algorithm]], which is an FPRAS for this problem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Karp |first1=Richard M |last2=Luby |first2=Michael |last3=Madras |first3=Neal |date=1989-09-01 |title=Monte-Carlo approximation algorithms for enumeration problems |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0196-6774%2889%2990038-2 |journal=Journal of Algorithms |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=429–448 |doi=10.1016/0196-6774(89)90038-2 |issn=0196-6774|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Tractable special cases ==

=== Affine constraint satisfaction problems ===

The variant of SAT corresponding to affine relations in the sense of [[Schaefer's dichotomy theorem]], i.e., where clauses amount to equations modulo 2 with the [[Exclusive or|XOR]] operator, is the only SAT variant for which the #SAT problem can be solved in polynomial time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Creignou |first1=Nadia |last2=Hermann |first2=Miki |date=1996-02-25 |title=Complexity of Generalized Satisfiability Counting Problems |journal=Information and Computation |volume=125 |issue=1 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1006/inco.1996.0016 |issn=0890-5401|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Bounded treewidth ===

If the instances to SAT are restricted using [[Graph (abstract data type)|graph]] parameters, the #SAT problem can become tractable. For instance, #SAT on SAT instances whose [[treewidth]] is bounded by a constant can be performed in [[polynomial time]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=FICHTE |first1=JOHANNES K. |last2=HECHER |first2=MARKUS |last3=THIER |first3=PATRICK |last4=WOLTRAN |first4=STEFAN |date=2021-03-12 |title=Exploiting Database Management Systems and Treewidth for Counting |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/s147106842100003x |journal=Theory and Practice of Logic Programming |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=128–157 |doi=10.1017/s147106842100003x |issn=1471-0684|arxiv=2001.04191 }}</ref> Here, the treewidth can be the primal treewidth, dual treewidth, or incidence treewidth of the [[hypergraph]] associated to the SAT formula, whose vertices are the variables and where each clause is represented as a hyperedge.

=== Restricted circuit and diagram classes ===

Model counting is tractable (solvable in polynomial time) for (ordered) [[binary decision diagram|BDDs]] and for some circuit formalisms studied in [[knowledge compilation]], such as [[d-DNNF]]s.

==Generalizations==

Weighted model counting (WMC) generalizes #SAT by computing a linear combination of the models instead of just counting the models. In the literal-weighted variant of WMC, each literal gets assigned a weight, such that
<math>\text{WMC}(\phi; w) = \sum_{M \models \phi} \prod_{l \in M} w(l)</math>.

WMC is used for probabilistic inference, as probabilistic queries over discrete random variables such as in [[Bayesian network]]s can be reduced to WMC.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chavira |first1=Mark |last2=Darwiche |first2=Adnan |title=On probabilistic inference by weighted model counting |journal=Artificial Intelligence |date=April 2008 |volume=172 |issue=6–7 |pages=772–799 |doi=10.1016/j.artint.2007.11.002}}</ref>

Algebraic model counting further generalizes #SAT and WMC over arbitrary commutative [[semirings]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kimmig |first1=Angelika |last2=Van den Broeck |first2=Guy |last3=De Raedt |first3=Luc |title=Algebraic model counting |journal=Journal of Applied Logic |date=July 2017 |volume=22 |pages=46–62 |doi=10.1016/j.jal.2016.11.031|arxiv=1211.4475 }}</ref>
